input: Representative sampling of a gas emission is a topic of considerable importance, because any measurement that is made on a gas stream can only ever be as good as the sample on which it is based. In order for a sample to be representative, it is essential that the samples are taken at a point where the emission stream is accessible and where the gas has had an opportunity to become thoroughly mixed, rather than at a point where the stream may still be stratified or disturbed. A sample, moreover, is not normally a single portion of gas collected on a single occasion; instead, it is built up from a number of increments that are collected at intervals over the period that the sample is intended to cover, and these increments are combined in order to form the one sample that is then analysed. A single grab sample, by contrast, captures the composition of the stream at one instant only, and it can therefore be seriously misleading, since the composition of a gas emission varies over time and a momentary sample may coincide with a peak, a dip, or a transient disturbance that the period as a whole does not resemble.
target:
Representative sampling of a gas emission rests on three choices: where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and over what period the increments are spread.

Samples are taken where the stream can be reached safely and where the gas is mixed. A stratified or disturbed stream gives different compositions at different points in the same cross-section, and a sample drawn from one point then describes that point rather than the emission. The sampling point is therefore chosen in a mixed region, and it is kept fixed, so that samples taken at different times differ because the emission differs, not because the sampling moved.

One sample is built from many increments, taken at intervals across the period the sample must represent and combined before analysis. A single grab sample holds the composition of one instant. Emissions vary over time, and an instant can fall on a peak, a dip, or a passing disturbance; the grab sample then reports that instant as if it were the period, and every quantity calculated from it inherits the error.

The increments are combined before analysis so that the laboratory receives the period, not a moment from it. Where increments cannot be combined, each is analysed and the results are averaged over the period; what matters is that no single instant stands for the whole. The sampling record states where the increments were taken and over what period, so that the result can be traced to the stream it claims to describe.
